attacks.claim: The public weekly open-data CSV publishes ward, zip, birth_year, gender, and created_at per response. Removing resident_id does not anonymize this: the combination of ward/zip, birth year, gender and timestamp is a classic quasi-identifier set, and in small zips it re-identifies individuals and their political preferences. Once published under CC-BY it cannot be recalled.
attacks.evidence: one CSV per poll on data.ourtown.org with columns ward, zip, birth_year, gender, ranking, verified, created_at. resident_id is removed before export.

attacks.claim: Demographics collected at optional verification for 'jury-pool-style demographic balance reports' are repurposed for publishing and for staff exports. This is a purpose change with no consent, and it conflicts with the anonymous-first/optional-verification commitment: verifying exposes more data than users agreed to.
attacks.evidence: address, zip, birth_year, gender (collected at optional verification for the jury-pool-style demographic balance reports)

attacks.claim: Plan buys the county voter file and uses it to send ~142,000 automated marketing/political-style SMS plus 3 reminders. Voter-file use is commonly restricted by state law to election/political/governmental purposes, and the plan does not check this. TCPA requires prior express consent for autodialed/automated texts to mobile numbers, and the exposure is statutory damages per message (about 568k messages). Twilio A2P 10DLC registration and carrier rules are also unaddressed, and a nonprofit using voter data for app growth is at legal and reputational risk. Opt-out is handled only via Twilio default STOP.
attacks.evidence: Purchase the county voter registration file from the County Clerk ($400, includes mobile numbers where provided). ... send an automated SMS to every registered voter ... then 3 automated reminders over 10 days.

attacks.claim: Voter-file PII (names, mobile numbers) is imported into the app and uploaded to a third party (Twilio) with no stated retention, deletion, access control, or consent. It is also linkable to poll participation via the link.
attacks.evidence: Load numbers into Twilio ... Week 4: voter-file import + SMS pipeline.

attacks.claim: The plan's own survey shows polls are the least-wanted feature (9%), while the top asks (council member votes and reasons 61%, neighborhood notifications 44%, summaries 37%) are not built. Yet Ward Voice is called the centerpiece and the whole 5-week build is spent on it. The plan does not reconcile this with the evidence, and the 'direct voice' claim is unsupported.
attacks.evidence: Polls on upcoming items — 9% ... is the centerpiece of the FY27 roadmap.

attacks.claim: The plan is solving the wrong problem. Residents asked for vote tracking, alerts and summaries. Staff's need for a structured way to hear from residents is anecdotal and is the only support for polls. The 30% new-user metric is served by mass SMS rather than by value to users.
attacks.evidence: Council staff have also told us they lack a structured way to hear from residents

attacks.claim: Integrity controls are weak. A device fingerprint is trivially evaded, the IP limit only queues responses over 3/min, and self-selected ward with no verification lets anyone stuff any ward. Staff gets no ability to remove responses, so abuse cannot be remediated. Mass SMS links to the first poll invite brigading, and the plan does not say how queued responses are reviewed or how many are expected.
attacks.evidence: 1 response per poll per device fingerprint ... unverified responses over 3/min from one IP are queued for review. / Staff cannot edit or delete responses

attacks.claim: A device fingerprint also constitutes tracking data that is not described in the data model (no column for it), so the rate-limit mechanism is not backed by the stated schema. Poll results derived from self-selected, unrepresentative responses are presented as per-ward sentiment next to council agenda items.
attacks.evidence: poll_responses(id, poll_id, resident_id null, ranking jsonb, ward, verified bool, created_at)

attacks.claim: The load target of 5k concurrent is untested, and an SMS blast to 142k people produces a spike with a link to a self-hosted Django stack. Load testing is left to week 5, the same week as launch.
attacks.evidence: Week 5: accessibility pass, load test (target 5k concurrent), launch.

attacks.claim: Twilio cost for ~568k messages is not budgeted; only the $400 file cost appears.

attacks.claim: A 'live' IRV tally on every view and weekly public export have no stated caching, failure handling, or monitoring. Accessibility is left to the final week, which risks late rework.
attacks.evidence: Week 3: IRV tally, results page, abuse controls.
